questions.stem: In which sentence is the article used correctly throughout?

options.option_text: She is an honest worker and an useful team member.
She is an honest worker and a useful team member.
She is a honest worker and an useful team member.
She is a honest worker and a useful team member.

questions.explanation: B is correct because article choice depends on the SOUND of the next word, not its spelling. 'Honest' has a silent 'h', so its first sound is the vowel /ɒ/, requiring 'an'. 'Useful' begins with /juː/ — a consonant sound — so it requires 'a'. Option A uses 'an useful', incorrectly treating the letter 'u' as always vowel-sounding. Option D fails on 'honest', using 'a' before a vowel sound.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence in which the preposition after 'different' is formally correct:

options.option_text: The outcome was quite different from what the committee had initially proposed.
The outcome was quite different than what the committee had initially proposed.
The outcome was quite different to what the committee had initially proposed.
The outcome was quite different with what the committee had initially proposed.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'different from' is the standard formal English construction endorsed in Indian competitive exam style guides. 'Different than' is used in informal American English. 'Different to' exists in British informal speech but is not accepted in formal examination writing. 'Different with' is entirely non-idiomatic and ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?

options.option_text: Walking along the shore, we spotted several dolphins leaping.
Having submitted the report, the project was considered complete.
Exhausted from the long journey, she fell asleep immediately.
After finishing lunch, the students resumed their afternoon classes.

questions.explanation: B contains a dangling modifier: 'Having submitted the report' implies a human agent submitted it, but the grammatical subject of the main clause is 'the project' — an inanimate noun that cannot perform the action. The participial phrase is therefore left without a logical referent. Options A, C, and D correctly pair their introductory phrases with the intended human subject immediately after the comma.

questions.stem: A student says: 'I will finish this assignment by tomorrow.' Which reported speech version is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: She said she will finish the assignment by tomorrow.
She said she would finish the assignment by the following day.
She said she would finish this assignment by tomorrow.
She told she would finish the assignment by the following day.

questions.explanation: B is correct: reported speech requires (i) tense backshift — 'will' becomes 'would', and (ii) time-adverb shift — 'tomorrow' becomes 'the following day'. Option A retains 'will' without backshift. Option C correctly shifts 'will' to 'would' but leaves 'tomorrow' unchanged, which is non-standard in formal indirect speech. Option D uses 'told' without a required indirect object — 'told me/him/her' is obligatory.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly maintains parallel structure with infinitive phrases?

options.option_text: The manager expects the team to meet deadlines, maintaining quality, and show initiative.
The manager expects the team to meet deadlines, maintain quality, and show initiative.
The manager expects the team meeting deadlines, to maintain quality, and show initiative.
The manager expects team to meeting deadlines, maintaining quality, showing initiative.

questions.explanation: B is correct: parallel structure after 'expects the team to' requires all items to use bare infinitives — 'to meet, (to) maintain, (to) show'. Option A mixes an infinitive with a gerund ('maintaining') and an infinitive, breaking parallelism. Option C opens the series with a gerund phrase. Option D uses 'to meeting', incorrectly combining the infinitive marker 'to' with a gerund — a structural error examiners frequently test.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the mandative subjunctive after a verb of insistence?

options.option_text: The committee insisted that the delegate submits a written apology.
The committee insisted that the delegate submit a written apology.
The committee insisted that the delegate submitted a written apology.
The committee insisted that the delegate would submit a written apology.

questions.explanation: B is correct: after verbs of demand, insistence, or recommendation (insist, demand, suggest, recommend), formal English uses the mandative subjunctive — the base form of the verb regardless of person or number ('submit', not 'submits'). Option A incorrectly applies the third-person singular '-s' inflection as though it were a normal present tense. Option C uses the simple past ('submitted'), not the subjunctive base form. Option D introduces a modal ('would'), which is non-standard in mandative subjunctive constructions.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies subject-auxiliary inversion after an initial negative adverbial?

options.option_text: Hardly had she spoken when the lights went out suddenly.
Hardly she had spoken when the lights went out suddenly.
Hardly did she speak when the lights went out suddenly.
Hardly she spoke when suddenly the lights had gone out.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Hardly...when' expresses two closely sequenced past events; it requires the past perfect with inverted auxiliary — 'Hardly had + subject + past participle'. Option B omits inversion entirely ('she had spoken' instead of 'had she spoken'). Option C applies simple-past inversion with 'did', but 'hardly...when' specifically demands the past perfect auxiliary 'had', not 'did'. Option D inverts nothing, misplaces 'suddenly', and wrongly shifts the past perfect to the wrong clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence demonstrates correct subject-verb agreement with a quantifier phrase?

options.option_text: The quality of the products have improved significantly this year.
Each of the boys were given a separate seat in the examination hall.
The number of applicants has increased threefold in recent years.
A large number of students was present during the annual function.

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'the number of' is a singular subject phrase and takes the singular verb 'has'. Option D is the most tempting distractor: 'a large number of' behaves as a plural quantifier and requires the plural verb 'were', not 'was'. Option A is wrong because the head noun 'quality' (singular) demands 'has improved', not 'have improved'. Option B is wrong because 'each' is always singular and demands 'was given'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the Present Perfect tense correctly in accordance with standard grammar rules?

options.option_text: She has gone to the market an hour ago and returned just now.
The team has already submitted the report to the committee.
He has lived in this city since three years without any break.
They have met the director yesterday to discuss the new project.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'already' is a standard adverb used with the present perfect to signal a recently completed action with present relevance. Option A is wrong because the time expression 'an hour ago' marks a definite past point, which requires the simple past ('went'), not the present perfect. Option C wrongly pairs 'since' with a duration ('three years'); 'since' requires a point in time, while 'for' is used with durations. Option D is wrong because 'yesterday' is a definite past marker that demands simple past ('met').

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund or infinitive after the governing verb?

options.option_text: She regretted to miss the opening ceremony of the cultural festival.
The officer denied having received any bribe from the contractor.
The committee suggested to revise the entire draft of the policy.
He avoided to travel during peak hours on the city metro railway.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'deny' always takes a gerund object ('deny doing/having done'). Option A is the most tempting distractor: 'regret + to-infinitive' exists but is restricted to formal announcements of present/future bad news ('I regret to inform you...'); for looking back on a past missed event, 'regretted missing' is required. Options C and D are wrong because 'suggest' and 'avoid' are both gerund-only verbs — 'suggested revising' and 'avoided travelling' are the correct forms.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correctly structured cleft sentence that appropriately highlights the focused element?

options.option_text: It is hard work that makes successful a person in competitive exams.
It was the principal who announced the new examination schedule.
It is my brother whom passed the UPSC civil services examination.
It was in college when she first learned to speak fluent English.

questions.explanation: B is correct: a cleft sentence follows the pattern 'It + be + [focused element] + relative clause', and 'It was the principal who announced…' correctly fronts the NP 'the principal' with the relative pronoun 'who'. Option C is the most tempting distractor — 'whom' looks formal but is wrong because it functions as the subject of 'passed', which requires the nominative 'who'. Option A has an inverted word order ('makes successful a person' instead of 'makes a person successful'). Option D wrongly uses 'when' instead of 'that' as the linker in an adverbial cleft.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly expresses an unreal past condition combined with a present-time result (mixed conditional)?

options.option_text: If she had studied harder, she would pass the examination easily.
If I had taken that job offer, I would be living abroad right now.
Had she worked diligently, she would have got a much better position.
If he studies regularly, he will definitely crack the SSC CGL exam.

questions.explanation: B is correct: the mixed conditional combines a Type 3 if-clause (past perfect: 'had taken') to signal an unreal past event with a Type 2 main clause (would + present continuous: 'would be living') to indicate the present consequence — the hallmark of a mixed conditional. Option A incorrectly mixes past perfect in the if-clause with a plain 'would + base' main clause, omitting the present-time signal; it would need 'would have passed' for a pure Type 3. Option C is a pure Type 3 conditional (past→past), not a mixed one. Option D is a Type 1 conditional expressing a real/possible future condition.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a correctly formed absolute phrase (nominative absolute construction)?

options.option_text: Weather permitting, the annual sports day will be held outdoors.
The task completing, the team celebrated their remarkable success.
His leg fracturing, the athlete withdrew from the championship finals.
The speech delivering, the minister left the auditorium immediately.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'weather permitting' is a standard absolute phrase formed with a noun + present participle denoting a simultaneous condition, and is fully idiomatic. Options B, C, and D all share the same error: they use present participles ('completing', 'fracturing', 'delivering') for actions that are logically completed before the main clause action — these must be past participles ('the task completed', 'his leg fractured', 'the speech delivered'). Option C is the most tempting distractor because an injury sounds like an ongoing process, but the withdrawal implies the fracture had already occurred, requiring the past participial form.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an abbreviated agreement structure with 'so' or 'neither' to echo a preceding clause?

options.option_text: Ravi can speak French fluently, and so does his younger sister too.
The director did not attend the meeting, and neither did the board.
She has finished her project already, and so have done her classmates.
He was not present at the function, and neither was not his assistant.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'neither + auxiliary + subject' mirrors the negative main clause; the echo auxiliary must match the tense and type of the original ('did not attend' → 'neither did the board'). Option A is the most tempting distractor: 'so + auxiliary + subject' is the correct affirmative echo structure, but the auxiliary must match — 'can speak' requires 'so can his sister', not 'so does'. The error of copying the wrong auxiliary (does vs. can) is a frequent exam trap. Option C inserts a redundant 'done' ('so have done' should simply be 'so have her classmates'). Option D creates a double negative with 'neither was not', which is ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies the distinction between 'fewer' and 'less' in accordance with standard grammar rules?

options.option_text: We received less enquiries this year compared to the previous one.
The clinic sees fewer patients on public holidays than on weekdays.
There is fewer traffic on the highway after ten o'clock at night.
She spends fewer money on transport since shifting to her new flat.

questions.explanation: 'Fewer' modifies countable nouns; 'less' modifies uncountable (mass) nouns. 'Patients' is countable, so 'fewer patients' in B is correct. Option A wrongly uses 'less' with the countable noun 'enquiries.' Option C uses 'fewer' with the uncountable 'traffic' — it should be 'less traffic.' Option D pairs 'fewer' with the uncountable 'money' — it should be 'less money.'

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct comparative or superlative form of the adjective?

options.option_text: This is the most worst performance I have ever witnessed on stage.
Of the three highways, the eastern route is the longest and smoothest.
She is the more talented of the three shortlisted candidates here.
The new machine is more faster and quieter than the older model.

questions.explanation: When comparing more than two items, the superlative ('longest', 'smoothest') is required, making B correct. Option A is the most tempting distractor — 'most worst' is a double superlative error since 'worst' is already a superlative. Option C incorrectly uses the comparative 'more talented' for a group of three; the superlative 'most talented' is needed. Option D creates the redundant form 'more faster' — 'faster' is already comparative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly handles verb agreement with a correlative conjunction pair according to the proximity rule?

options.option_text: Neither the principal nor the teachers was satisfied with the outcome.
Either the manager or the clerk has misplaced the official files.
Not only the students but also the professor were given a prize.
Both the chairman as well as the secretary have signed the letter.

questions.explanation: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. In B, the nearer subject is 'clerk' (singular), so 'has' is correct. Option A has 'teachers' (plural) as the nearer subject, so 'was' should be 'were.' Option C has 'professor' (singular) nearest to the verb, so 'were' should be 'was' — the most tempting error because 'students' (plural) appears earlier. Option D misuses 'both...as well as'; 'both' must pair with 'and', not 'as well as.'

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies the sequence of tenses in a complex sentence governed by a past-tense main verb?

options.option_text: The officer said that the inquiry committee will submit its report shortly.
The manager realised that the accounts team had made a serious error.
He declared that all the pending files are to be cleared by Friday.
She told the examiner that she forgets to bring her hall ticket.

questions.explanation: B correctly uses the past perfect 'had made' to indicate an action that preceded the past-tense 'realised.' Option A retains 'will' in the subordinate clause after the past verb 'said' — it must backshift to 'would.' Option C keeps the present 'are' after the past verb 'declared'; it should be 'were.' Option D uses the present 'forgets' after the past 'told' — the most common exam trap here, since candidates confuse subordinate-clause tense shift with a general-truth exception.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'who', 'whom', 'whoever', or 'whomever' in accordance with formal grammar conventions?

options.option_text: The analyst who the board appointed resigned within three months.
Please forward the application to whoever is heading the department.
She is the officer whom filed the complaint against the contractor.
We shall interview whoever you recommend for the senior position.

questions.explanation: In B, 'whoever' is the subject of 'is heading' inside the embedded clause; the preposition 'to' governs the entire clause, not the pronoun directly, so the subjective form 'whoever' is correct. Option A needs 'whom' — the pronoun is the object of 'appointed.' Option C needs 'who' — it is the subject of 'filed,' not an object. Option D is the key distractor: 'whoever' must be 'whomever' because within the embedded clause it is the object of 'recommend.'

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the past subjunctive in a 'wish' or 'if only' construction as required by formal grammar?

options.option_text: I wish I was able to attend the national conference on linguistics.
She wishes she were fluent in Mandarin before the diplomatic summit.
If only the minister was aware of the actual ground conditions here.
He wishes the examination was scheduled for a different time slot.

questions.explanation: After 'wish' and 'if only', formal grammar requires the past subjunctive 'were' for all persons — including 'she', 'I', and 'he' — to mark a contrary-to-fact hypothesis. B correctly uses 'were fluent.' Option A ('I wish I was') is the most tempting distractor: the indicative 'was' sounds natural in informal speech but violates the subjunctive requirement. Options C and D commit the same indicative-for-subjunctive substitution after 'if only' and 'wishes' respectively.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly applies subject-verb concord involving the expressions 'the number of' or 'a number of'?

options.option_text: A number of candidates was disqualified for submitting forged certificates.
The number of registered voters have increased since the last election.
A number of complaints have been received against the new regulation.
The number of pending cases were reduced after the new judge's order.

questions.explanation: 'A number of' functions like 'several/many' and takes a plural verb; 'the number of' treats 'number' as the singular head noun and takes a singular verb. C is correct: 'a number of complaints have been received' rightly uses the plural verb. Option A uses the singular 'was' with 'a number of' — the single most frequent exam error on this point. Options B and D use plural verbs ('have increased', 'were reduced') with 'the number of', which is singular and requires 'has increased' and 'was reduced' respectively.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly to show possession?

options.option_text: The committee's report was submitted on time.
The committee's report were submitted on time.
The committees report was submitted on time.
The committees' report were submitted on time.

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'committee's' (singular possessive) pairs correctly with the singular verb 'was'. Option D uses 'committees'' (plural possessive) suggesting multiple committees, but then incorrectly uses 'were' instead of matching with a clear subject. Option C omits the apostrophe entirely, making it a noun adjunct rather than possessive.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a reflexive pronoun?

options.option_text: The manager asked my colleague and myself to lead the audit.
The director himself reviewed every single draft clause.
Please send the report to myself at the earliest opportunity.
Herself completed the application without any assistance at all.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'himself' is used as an intensive reflexive, emphasising that the director personally reviewed the drafts — a legitimate intensifier use. Options A and C misuse 'myself' as a polite substitute for 'me', which is grammatically incorrect; 'myself' requires a prior 'I' as antecedent in the same clause. Option D uses 'Herself' as a sentence subject, which is ungrammatical.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a non-restrictive relative clause with appropriate punctuation?

options.option_text: The policy that was amended last year has improved output.
The river Ganga, that originates in Uttarakhand, is sacred.
My eldest sister, who lives in Pune, is a cardiologist.
The students who passed the exam they deserve a reward.

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'who lives in Pune' is a non-restrictive clause adding extra information about a uniquely identified person ('my eldest sister'), correctly set off by commas and using 'who'. Option B wrongly uses 'that' in a non-restrictive clause — 'that' cannot introduce non-restrictive clauses; 'which' is required. Option A is a correctly punctuated restrictive clause (no commas, using 'that'), but the stem asks for a non-restrictive example. Option D inserts the redundant pronoun 'they', making it a run-on.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly employs the passive voice with a retained object?

options.option_text: The students were given the scholarship by the foundation board.
The scholarship was given to the students by foundation board.
The scholarship given to the students by the foundation board.
The students given the scholarship by the foundation board members.

questions.explanation: A is correct: with a ditransitive verb like 'give', the indirect object ('the students') can become the passive subject while the direct object ('the scholarship') is retained — this is the retained-object passive. Option B promotes the direct object to subject, which is also grammatically possible but changes focus and drops the article before 'foundation'; more critically it omits 'the' before 'foundation board', making it ungrammatical. Options C and D lack an auxiliary verb ('were'/'was'), producing verbless fragments.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a participle phrase without creating a misrelated participle error?

options.option_text: Walking through the market, several rare spices caught my eye.
Having submitted the petition, the villagers awaited the verdict.
Exhausted from the trek, the tent was set up immediately by us.
Analysing the data carefully, errors were found in the report.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Having submitted the petition' logically attaches to 'the villagers' — the same entity performed both actions. Option A is a dangling modifier: 'spices' cannot be 'walking'. Option C attaches 'Exhausted' to 'the tent', which is absurd. Option D implies the errors were analysing the data, another dangling modifier. The critical test is whether the participial phrase's implied subject matches the main clause's grammatical subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly distinguishes between 'lie' (to recline) and 'lay' (to place) across tenses?

options.option_text: He laid on the bench for an hour and then sat up slowly.
She lay the documents on the desk before the meeting began.
The injured worker had lain in the corridor for twenty minutes.
They have laid down exhausted after the twelve-hour shift ended.

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'lain' is the past participle of 'lie' (intransitive, to recline), so 'had lain' is perfectly formed. Option A uses 'laid' (past of 'lay', which requires an object) intransitively — wrong; should be 'lay'. Option B uses 'lay' (past of 'lie') where 'laid' (past of 'lay' with object 'documents') is needed. Option D uses 'laid down' intransitively meaning to recline, but 'laid' requires an object; the correct past participle here is 'lain' — 'have lain down exhausted'. The lie/lay paradigm (lie–lay–lain vs. lay–laid–laid) is a classic high-frequency PYQ trap.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an elliptical clause without creating a faulty comparison or incomplete structure?

options.option_text: The scores of Team A are higher than Team B in every round.
Ravi writes more fluently than any other student in his batch.
Her knowledge of taxation is greater than her colleagues clearly.
This engine performs better than any engine ever manufactured.

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'than any other student' correctly excludes Ravi from the comparison group via 'other', preventing the illogical reading 'more fluent than himself'. Option A compares 'scores of Team A' with 'Team B' (an entity, not scores) — a faulty parallel comparison; should be 'than those of Team B'. Option C omits 'that of' before 'her colleagues', making it compare knowledge to persons. Option D omits 'other', producing the self-inclusion paradox (this engine is better than itself). The 'any other' rule and parallel comparison structure are among the most frequently tested hard-grammar angles.
